SSRI Adverse Effects

name the effect, then take the next stepDid it start on the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Clonus hyperreflexia mydriasis within hours of adding or raising a serotonergic drug serotonin syndrome
  • FINISH symptoms typically within 3 days of a stop or taper discontinuation; relapse typically comes 2 to 3 weeks or more after
  • Low desire, persistent and distressing lower the dose first; then taper off, or add or switch to bupropion or mirtazapine
What it is

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI): citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline

Mechanism

Serotonin transporter blocked more serotonin in the cleft longer postsynaptic stimulation Drug detailSerotonin type 2 receptor stimulation commonly causes anxiety, insomnia and sexual dysfunction. Little effect on dopamine or norepinephrine.

Used for

Guideline detailAbout as effective as bupropion, mirtazapine, SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) or trazodone.

Panic disorder: a first-line drug, with or without CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy)

Bulimia nervosa: fluoxetine cuts binges and vomiting

Risks

Serotonin syndrome with another serotonergic drug, eg, an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor), tramadol, linezolid

Suicidal thoughts in children and young adults under 25 (boxed warning)

Hyponatremia, often from SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), higher risk over 65

Citalopram: more TermThe QT is the electrocardiogram interval of ventricular depolarization and repolarization. prolongation than other SSRIs; generally avoided after a recent MI (myocardial infarction)

Sexual dysfunction In practiceIn practice: the Merck Manual reports sexual dysfunction in more than half of patients.

Paroxetine: avoided in pregnancy (first-trimester cardiac malformations); most discontinuation symptoms

Bleeding, including GI bleeding, more with aspirin, an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or an anticoagulant

Insights

Reflexes split the two toxic syndromes: clonus and hyperreflexia in serotonin syndrome; slow reflexes and lead-pipe rigidity in neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Shorter half-life more withdrawal: paroxetine most, fluoxetine least fluoxetine may replace a drug whose slow taper fails

Adverse effects, by time coursedetail behind the risks
HoursSerotonin syndrome after a serotonergic change, about 60% within 6 hours; discontinuation reactions reported within hours of a first missed dose
OngoingSexual dysfunction in up to half (especially trouble reaching orgasm; also low libido, erectile dysfunction); sleep disturbance; weight change
StoppingDiscontinuation typically within 3 days, over in 1 to 2 weeks; relapse typically 2 to 3 weeks or more after, and graduala gradual taper leaves as few as 5% with symptoms
Older adultsParoxetine: more anticholinergic effects; fluoxetine: more agitation and overstimulation; neither is advisedsertraline or escitalopram are good first choices
2Urgent risks
ToxicitySerotonin syndrome: mental status change, sweating, shivering, hyperthermia, mydriasis, tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, increased bowel sounds
Severe cases≥41.1 °C needs sedation and intubation; antipyretics such as acetaminophen do not work. Guideline detailThe Hunter criteria are recommended as the most accurate. Drug detailCitalopram prolongs the QT interval more than other SSRIs. SSRIs have a wide safety margin: overdose is rarely dangerous, unlike a TCA (tricyclic antidepressant) overdose. A citalopram overdose can still cause torsade de pointes; monitor the heart for longer.

If clonus and hyperreflexia appear within hours of adding or raising a serotonergic drug, choose serotonin syndrome: stop every serotonergic drug.

OverdoseSSRI overdose with drowsiness, slow breathing or an abnormal exam
An SSRI alone is usually well tolerated

If an SSRI overdose comes with altered mental status or abnormal findings, choose a search for coingestants, such as acetaminophen, salicylate and ethanol levels.

SuicideNew suicidal thoughts or clinical worsening on an antidepressant
Risk raised in children and young adults in short-term studies

If any patient is on an antidepressant, choose close monitoring for worsening and suicidal thoughts.

PregnancyAn SSRI in pregnancy
Paroxetine: first-trimester cardiac malformations Guideline detailBreastfeeding can be encouraged on an antidepressant.

If a pregnant patient needs an SSRI, choose sertraline or escitalopram, good first choices; not paroxetine.

3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
Discontinuation syndrome In a vignetteThe trigger: she has discontinued the dosage of her sertraline during the past monthHyperarousal: mild tremor in both handsFINISH symptoms, electric-shock sensations after a stop, taper or missed doseTypically within 3 days; gone in 1 to 2 weeks; clonus or hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome instead
Low mood, insomnia and psychomotor symptoms returnTypically 2 to 3 weeks or longer after stopping; builds gradually
Serotonin syndromeMental status change, autonomic hyperactivity, clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, increased bowel soundsMinutes to hours after adding or raising a serotonergic drug; about 60% within 6 hours
On an antipsychotic: fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, ↑ CK (creatine kinase)Days to weeks after an antipsychotic change; builds over 1 to 3 days; slow reflexes, rigidity
Low libido, erectile dysfunction or anorgasmiaDuring therapy; name the phase: desire, arousal or orgasm; Timing often points to the SSRIDepression's own sexual symptoms should lift with the mood. Bupropion does not cause sexual dysfunction. Female sexual interest/arousal disorder needs 6 months or more and no drug or medical cause. Stable diabetes, high blood pressure or obesity is less likely to explain a recent change.Gynecomastia is uncommon on an SSRI; see
Early activationAnxiety, insomniaAt the start, before any benefit; especially troubling in panic disorder
FINISH
  • F – flu-like symptoms: fatigue, lethargy, malaise, muscle aches, headaches, diarrhea
  • I – insomnia
  • N – nausea
  • I – imbalance: gait instability, dizziness or lightheadedness, vertigo
  • S – sensory disturbances: paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, visual disturbance
  • H – hyperarousal: anxiety, agitation
Pause point
New symptoms 2 days after a stop Offered as relapse, so a new antidepressant is started Relapse typically arrives weeks later and builds slowly → That timing is discontinuation
Low desire on an SSRI; depression in sustained remission Offered as switching to citalopram or a weekend drug holiday The optionsInitiate propranolol: an add-on that leaves the antidepressant alone; but it is unlikely to help sexual dysfunction and is not helpful for major depressive disorder.
Initiate sildenafil: a treatment for sexual dysfunction; but it can help arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire, her complaint, has been shown.
Recommend weekend drug holidays: they seem to spare the relationship; but they are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect.
Replace fluoxetine with citalopram: a switch sounds like progress; but citalopram carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction.
Down to two: lowering the dose or switching to citalopram. Lower the dose: her low desire is persistent and distressing, and NBME says initial management commonly involves decreasing the SSRI dose, especially with sustained remission. If that fails: one episode in sustained remission, so stopping can be considered; or, if she prefers to stay on medication, adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine). Citalopram carries a similar risk; holidays interfere with the antidepressant effect → Lower the dose first
7Treatment
Manage by effect
EffectDoAvoid
Low desire, persistent and distressingLower the dose first (ladder below)Weekend drug holidays; propranolol; another SSRI such as citalopram (similar risk)
Arousal problems or anorgasmiaSildenafil can helpThe same drug for low desire: no effect shown
Serotonin syndromeStop every serotonergic drug; IV fluids and oxygen; a benzodiazepine; if those fail, cyproheptadine (evidence inconclusive)Antipyretics for the fever: they do not work
A switch is needed, but bulimia or seizure riskMirtazapine: fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs (watch appetite and weight gain): contraindicated
FINISH symptoms days after a stopExclude other serious causes, then reassure (ladder below)A new antidepressant for presumed relapse
Early activation, eg, in panic disorderHalf the usual depression starting dose; raise about every 7 days; if it appears, lower the dose or change the SSRIThe full starting dose

Low desire on an SSRI

1

First steplow desire is persistent and distressing

Lower the SSRI dose

With the depression in sustained remission.

2

If a lower dose failsone episode, in sustained remission, and willing to stop

Consider stopping, by taper

Taper gradually, typically over 6 to 8 weeks; never stop abruptly.

3

Or, if a lower dose failswants to stay on an antidepressant to prevent another episode, or has had 2 or more episodes

Add bupropion, or switch to bupropion or mirtazapine

Watch forOne of very few antidepressants without sexual dysfunction; lowers the seizure threshold. Contraindicated with a seizure disorder, bulimia or anorexia. Watch forFewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs; drowsiness, a bigger appetite and weight gain.

Discontinuation symptoms

1

Every patientother serious causes ruled out

Reassure: reversible, not dangerous, over in 1 to 2 weeks

Then consider a restart with a slow taper, or support if the patient prefers not to restart. Guideline detailIt may be misread as stroke, another neurologic illness, an infection or another drug's adverse effect.

2

During a tapersymptoms began while tapering

Consider the original dose again, then a slower taper
3

Taper not tolerateda slow taper is poorly tolerated

Consider substituting fluoxetine, with its longer half-life
8Follow-up
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Before startingBipolar disorder, mania or hypomania in the patient or a relativeIn bipolar disorder, an antidepressant alone can set off mania
2 to 4 weeks after starting, older adultsSerum sodiumSIADH, higher risk over 65; ask about past hyponatremia before starting
Up to 6 weeks inResponseBenefit may take that long
Mood rises after startingMania or hypomania (rare)If it appears: stop the antidepressant and start a mood stabilizer
Remission of a first episodeContinue about 6 more months at the dose that brought remission, then taper gradually, typically over 6 to 8 weeks (about 2 months)Lowering or stopping sooner raises the risk of relapse Guideline detailRecurrent, chronic or severe depression: consider maintenance at the remission dose, usually for 1 to 3 years or longer, sometimes indefinitely.
Interactions
WithEffectDo
Tramadol, linezolid, a triptan, meperidine, dextromethorphan, ondansetron or St John's wortSerotonin syndromeWatch for clonus and hyperreflexia within hours of the change; avoid St John's wort
Serotonin syndrome, potentially life-threateningSwitching to an MAOI: stop the SSRI and wait 5 weeks after fluoxetine, 2 weeks after other antidepressants
Aspirin, NSAIDs, warfarin or another anticoagulantMore bleeding, including GI: SSRIs block serotonin uptake into platelets, which need it for hemostasisWarn of bleeding; on warfarin, monitor the INR (international normalized ratio)
Drugs cleared by liver cytochrome P450 enzymes, eg, tamoxifen, TCAs, metoprolol, tizanidine, theophylline, clozapine↑ or ↓ levels; paroxetine has the most drug interactions, citalopram the fewestCheck the combination before starting Drug detailTamoxifen: paroxetine, a strong inhibitor of CYP2D6 (a cytochrome P450 enzyme), lowers its active metabolite, and fluoxetine is also a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor; consider an antidepressant with little CYP2D6 inhibition. Drugs cleared by CYP2D6, such as TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants) and metoprolol: ↑ levels, most with paroxetine and fluoxetine (citalopram inhibits weakly); lower their dose if needed. Fluvoxamine strongly inhibits CYP1A2 (cytochrome P450 1A2): never with tizanidine; lower the theophylline dose; clozapine levels may rise.
Practice
  1. 34-year-old man, one depressive episode in remission 7 months on sertraline 150 mg daily low sexual desire since starting it it is straining his marriage no suicidal ideation · euthymic, full affect, linear thought · HR 72/min, BP 124/76 mm Hg → Lower the sertraline dose → persistent, distressing low desire in sustained remission: lowering the dose is the common first step; drug holidays are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect
  2. 31-year-old man, one moderate depressive episode in remission 10 months on sertraline dose cut from 150 to 100 mg 2 months ago for low desire still distressed; would rather stop euthymic, full affect, linear thought · no suicidal ideation · HR 70/min → Taper sertraline off gradually → a lower dose failed, and one episode in sustained remission allows stopping; an SSRI is tapered, not stopped abruptly
  3. 27-year-old woman, one depressive episode, in remission 14 months escitalopram lowered 8 weeks ago for low desire desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant No seizures, eating disorder or heart disease euthymic, reactive affect · HR 68/min → Add bupropion to escitalopram → a lower dose failed and she prefers to stay on medication: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine); sildenafil has not been shown to affect desire
  4. 45-year-old man, one depressive episode, in remission 9 months sertraline cut 150 to 100 mg 3 months ago wants to stay on it desire intact; erection trouble since starting it; bothers him euthymic · HR 72/min, BP 126/80 mm Hg → Add sildenafil to sertraline → desire is intact and the problem is arousal, which sildenafil can help; propranolol is unlikely to help, and another SSRI carries a similar risk
  5. 24-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa one depressive episode, in remission on fluoxetine after a dose reduction, desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · HR 66/min · potassium 3.9 mEq/L · euthymic → Switching to bupropion → bupropion has no sexual adverse effects but is contraindicated in bulimia; mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs
  6. 38-year-old woman ran out of paroxetine 4 days ago after 2 years for remitted depression 2 days of nausea, dizziness, unsteady gait, poor sleep brief electric-shock sensations in arms T 37.0 °C · reflexes normal, no clonus · anxious, irritable; mood fine → SSRI discontinuation syndrome → FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping a short half-life drug; relapse comes 2 to 3 weeks or more later, and normal reflexes without clonus argue against serotonin syndrome
  7. 52-year-old man stopped sertraline on his own 3 days ago after 1 year; depression in remission mild nausea, lightheadedness, trouble sleeping wants to stay off T 36.9 °C · reflexes normal, no tremor or clonus · euthymic, mildly irritable · no suicidal ideation → Reassure; it resolves in 1 to 2 weeks → with other serious causes unlikely (afebrile, normal reflexes, no clonus), discontinuation symptoms after an abrupt stop: begin with reassurance that they are reversible and run their course in 1 to 2 weeks; restarting with a slow taper is considered, or support if he prefers not to restart
  8. 35-year-old woman, depression in remission 8 months 2 weeks into a paroxetine taper, 40 mg to 20 mg daily 3 days of dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations irritability keeps her from work T 37.1 °C · no clonus · anxious; mood not depressed → Resume 40 mg and taper more slowly → symptoms during a taper: consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly; fluoxetine is for a slow taper that is poorly tolerated
  9. 42-year-old man, depression in remission 1 year two tries to come off paroxetine, each tapered over 8 weeks both times: dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations relieved by resuming the full dose euthymic · no suicidal ideation · T 36.8 °C → Switch to fluoxetine, then stop → slow tapering is poorly tolerated: consider substituting fluoxetine, whose longer half-life makes discontinuation symptoms less likely
  10. 58-year-old woman taking sertraline got tramadol for back pain this morning 5 hours later: agitated, sweating, nauseated T 38.4 °C · HR 122/min · BP 162/94 mm Hg · dilated pupils · tremor, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus · hyperactive bowel sounds · oriented to person only → Serotonin syndrome → tramadol added to an SSRI, then clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis within hours; neuroleptic malignant syndrome builds over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes
  11. 29-year-old man stopped paroxetine for anxiety on his own 4 days ago 3 days of constant dizziness and nausea, worse when he turns his head achy and chilled; electric zaps in his head; tingling hands Afebrile · pupils and reflexes normal · no clonus → SSRI discontinuation syndrome → abruptly stopping a short half-life antidepressant such as paroxetine can bring flu-like, neurologic and psychiatric symptoms, typically within days, including electric shock-like sensations and paresthesias; benign paroxysmal positional vertigo brings minutes-long spells that resolve when holding still, not constant dizziness, and anxiety alone does not explain the flu-like and neurologic symptoms
Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: did the mood rise, not fall, after the SSRI started? (antidepressant-induced mania is rare). Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the anxiety new within 3 days of a stop, a hyperarousal symptom of discontinuation? Premenstrual Syndrome and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: when an SSRI treats a confirmed premenstrual syndrome.
Transferable rule

Name the effect and its timing before changing the drug. During therapy, with persistent, distressing low desire, lowering the dose is the common first step; typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper, think discontinuation, not relapse.
